title: How to Build AI Agent Integrations Once and Reuse Them Across Multiple Frameworks
summary: Building the same Slack, Gmail, GitHub, or CRM integration for every AI agent framework creates unnecessary authentication and maintenance work. Learn how to separate your integration layer from framework-specific adapters so you can build integrations once and reuse them across multiple frameworks.
body_text: Most teams do not set out to support more than one AI agent framework. It usually happens gradually. A prototype gets built in LangChain, a new product team prefers the Claude Agent SDK, another squad is experimenting with CrewAI, and somewhere along the way someone adds an MCP server for good measure. Each framework has its own way of defining tools, and each new tool means writing the Slack, Gmail, GitHub, or CRM integration all over again. This is the quiet tax of building AI agent integrations without a plan for reuse. The API you are calling has not changed. The auth flow has not changed. The data you are fetching has not changed. Only the wrapper around it has, and that wrapper gets rebuilt every single time a new framework enters the picture. This post walks through why that happens, what specifically gets duplicated, and how to structure your integrations so you write the logic once and plug it into any framework you use today or adopt later. Why Supporting Multiple AI Frameworks Can Mean Rebuilding the Same Integrations Every AI agent framework ships with its own concept of a "tool." LangChain has its tool decorators and BaseTool classes. CrewAI has its own Tool interface. The OpenAI Agents SDK defines function tools with a particular schema shape. The Claude Agent SDK expects tools registered in yet another format. None of these shapes are compatible with each other, even when the underlying action, say, searching Google Drive or posting to Slack, is identical. So when a team decides to support multi-framework AI agents, the natural first instinct is to treat each framework as its own project. That means a fresh Slack client for the LangChain build, a second Slack client for the Claude Agent SDK build, and a third if a CrewAI proof of concept gets greenlit. Three codebases now share zero integration code even though they are calling the same Slack endpoints with the same permissions. This pattern is easy to miss early on because a single integration for a single framework does not feel expensive. It only becomes a problem once you count how much of that code is identical across frameworks. Teams that have already gone deep on one AI agent framework, like the Claude Agent SDK integrations covered in this developer guide , often run into this exact wall the moment a second framework enters the stack. What Actually Gets Duplicated When You Build Integrations for Each AI Framework? If you strip away the framework specific wrapper, the actual work inside most integrations looks almost identical no matter which agent framework is calling it. Here is what typically gets rebuilt, line for line, every time: OAuth flows and consent screens for each connected service Token storage and token refresh logic so credentials do not silently expire Pagination handling for endpoints that return large result sets Retry logic and rate limit handling for APIs that throttle or fail intermittently Webhook signature verification and event parsing Data normalization so the agent gets a clean, consistent shape back Error handling that turns a raw API error into something the agent can reason about Permission and approval logic for actions that should not run without a human sign off None of this is specific to LangChain, CrewAI, or any other framework. It is specific to the third party API. A good example of just how much of this work lives outside the framework entirely is the OAuth walkthrough for connecting an agent to Gmail , which spends most of its time on consent screens, scope selection, and long term token management rather than anything related to a specific agent framework. That complexity exists whether the agent calling Gmail is built in LangChain or the Claude Agent SDK, which is exactly why rebuilding it per framework is such an expensive habit. How Framework-Specific Tooling Creates More Integration Code, Authentication Logic, and Maintenance Work The duplication problem gets worse once you look at how tightly most teams couple business logic to a framework's tool definition. A common pattern looks like this: the function that calls the Slack API, the function that formats the response for the agent, and the framework specific tool registration all live in the same file. That might seem convenient at first, but it means the auth handling and the framework adapter are welded together. The result is that every new AI agent framework you adopt requires touching authentication logic again, even though nothing about the credentials themselves has changed. A team that already built a working Google Drive integration for one framework, as shown in this walkthrough on connecting Google Drive to the OpenAI Agents SDK , typically has to redo the OAuth scoping, service account handling, and query construction from scratch if they later want the same capability inside a different framework. The Drive API has not changed. The scopes have not changed. Only the tool registration syntax has, and that alone should not require rewriting the whole integration. This is where maintenance cost compounds. A policy change from a provider, a deprecated API version, or a new required scope now needs to be patched in two or three places instead of one, and it is easy for one of those copies to quietly fall out of date while the others get updated. What Should You Separate From Your AI Framework to Make Integrations Reusable? The fix is not a new framework. It is a boundary. If you want reusable AI integrations, the work needs to be split into two distinct layers that do not know about each other: The integration layer : everything that talks to the third party API. Credential and token management, request construction, retries, rate limit handling, pagination, webhook processing, and permission checks all live here. The framework adapter layer : a thin wrapper that takes what the integration layer already does and exposes it in whatever shape a given AI agent framework expects for a tool. The test for whether you have drawn this line correctly is simple. If you added a brand new AI agent framework to your stack tomorrow, would you need to touch anything related to authentication, retries, or data shape? If the answer is yes, those concerns are still tangled up with the framework instead of separated from it. Concretely, that means separating out: Credential storage and refresh, independent of any framework Request and retry logic, independent of any framework The data shape returned to the caller, independent of any framework Permission and approval rules, independent of any framework Webhook and event handling, independent of any framework Once those pieces exist on their own, the framework specific code shrinks down to almost nothing: a name, a description, an input schema, and a single function call into the integration layer. How to Build a Framework Agnostic Integration Layer for Your AI Agents In practice, a framework agnostic integration layer is just a normal, typed client library that has no idea an AI agent will ever call it. It exposes plain functions. Those functions handle auth, retries, and normalization internally, and they return clean, predictable data. Nothing about them references LangChain, CrewAI, MCP, or any other framework. Here is a simplified example of what that looks like in TypeScript AI integrations built this way: // integrations/github.ts import { github } from '@corsair-dev/github'; import { createCorsair } from 'corsair/core'; const corsair = createCorsair({ plugins: [github()], }); export async function getOpenPullRequests(repo: string) { return corsair.github.api.pulls.list({ repo, state: 'open' }); } Notice that this file never mentions an agent, a tool, or a framework. It is just a function that returns open pull requests, with auth, token refresh, and retries handled underneath it. Whether that data is fetched by way of an API sprawling across dozens of quirky endpoints like the ones described in this breakdown of how Google APIs actually handle auth and rate limits , or a simpler service, the pattern is the same: the integration layer absorbs the complexity so nothing above it has to. This is really what an AI integration layer, or an AI agent integration layer more specifically, is for. It sits between your agents and the outside world, and it is the single place where "how do we talk to GitHub" gets answered, once. How to Reuse the Same Integrations Across AI Frameworks Without Rebuilding Your Tools With the integration layer in place, cross framework AI integrations become a matter of writing a small adapter, not a new integration. Each framework gets a thin file that maps its tool format onto the function you already wrote. For LangChain: // adapters/langchain.ts import { tool } from '@langchain/core/tools'; import { getOpenPullRequests } from '../integrations/github'; export const githubPRTool = tool( async ({ repo }) => JSON.stringify(await getOpenPullRequests(repo)), { name: 'get_open_pull_requests', description: 'List open pull requests for a given repository', } ); For the Claude Agent SDK: // adapters/claude-agent-sdk.ts import { getOpenPullRequests } from '../integrations/github'; export const githubPRTool = { name: 'get_open_pull_requests', description: 'List open pull requests for a given repository', input_schema: { type: 'object', properties: { repo: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['repo'], }, handler: async ({ repo }: { repo: string }) => getOpenPullRequests(repo), }; Both adapters call the exact same function. Neither one contains a single line of auth handling, retry logic, or data normalization, because that work already happened once inside the integration layer. Add a third AI agent framework next quarter, and the only new code needed is another small adapter file, not another rebuild of GitHub, Slack, or Gmail from scratch. That is the practical payoff of framework agnostic integrations. You are no longer choosing between AI agent frameworks and rebuilding your tools every time you change your mind or your product needs a second one running alongside the first. You build the integration once, keep it accurate as providers change their APIs, and let every framework you use today or add tomorrow plug into the same layer.

title: Hafnia Wins Danish Shipping Diversity Award 2026
summary: Hafnia has been named the winner of the Danish Shipping Diversity Award 2026. This year’s award, themed “Small changes, big impact,” recognizes smaller initiatives that make a difference in organizational culture and employees’ everyday working lives. Hafnia was honoured in particular for its Seafarer Advisory Board, referenced by the judges as a model for […]
body_text: Hafnia has been named the winner of the Danish Shipping Diversity Award 2026. This year’s award, themed “Small changes, big impact,” recognizes smaller initiatives that make a difference in organizational culture and employees’ everyday working lives. Hafnia was honoured in particular for its Seafarer Advisory Board, referenced by the judges as a model for how crews and management can shape decisions together. Established in November 2024, the Seafarer Advisory Board is a formal forum that connects Hafnia’s crews directly with onshore management, ensuring operational decisions reflect the lived experience of those at sea. It has eight members – five seafarers from Hafnia’s in-house fleet and three from its technically outsourced fleet – so that perspectives are heard across the full operating model. The Board meets several times a year, and its input feeds directly into onboard decisions, from reviewing reporting procedures to simplifying risk assessments and improving day-to-day working conditions. “This award belongs to our seafarers,” said Ralph Juhl, EVP, Head of Technical at Hafnia. “The Advisory Board works because it takes the views of our people who run our vessels seriously – and gives them a direct line to the decisions that affect their working lives. Hopefully helping to create genuinely better conditions when working onboard Hafnia vessels.” Hafnia congratulates shortlisted nominees Unitankers and ESVAGT. The full press release on the nominations from Danish Shipping can be read here: https://danishshipping.dk/en/latest-news/2026/meet-the-nominees-for-the-danish-shipping-dei-award-2026/ The winner was announced at Danish Shipping’s annual Pride Bar event, and was received by Mia Krogslund Jørgensen, VP, Head of People, Culture & Strategy, and Mikkel Boesen, VP, Head of TECOS (Hafnia’s technically outsourced fleet). The recognition continues a strong record for Hafnia in diversity and inclusion. At the Danish Shipping Diversity Award, Hafnia previously won in 2022 for the Maritime DEI Lab and in 2024 for the Hafnia Culture Lab. In 2026, Hafnia has also been recognized with the Diversity & Inclusion Honours Award, presented during the High-Level Conference of the Cyprus EU Presidency, and the Crew Welfare Diversity & Inclusion Award from SAFETY4SEA. title: Does Hair Hydration Require More Than Just Water?
summary: Does water alone fix dry hair? Learn how hair hydration works and discover tips for better moisture retention and healthier-looking hair.
body_text: Hydration & Hair Health Effect of Dehydration on Hair Water vs Electrolytes Minerals for Hydrated Hair Signs of Under-Nourished Hair Busting Hair Care Myths Hair Care Routine for Hydrated Hair Dermatologist Consult for Persistently Dry Hair FAQs Water is essential for healthy hair, but it is not enough to keep hair hydrated on its own. While water is absorbed into the hair shaft, temporarily increasing its moisture content, long-term moisture balance depends on the hair's ability to retain water, which is influenced by cuticle condition, hair porosity, and exposure to damaging factors. Factors such as heat styling, chemical treatments, and environmental exposure can weaken the hair cuticle, making it easier for moisture to escape. In this blog, we will discuss how hair hydration works, whether water alone is enough to keep hair hydrated, the role of electrolytes and moisture-retaining ingredients, common signs of dehydrated hair, and practical tips to maintain soft, smooth, and healthy-looking hair. How Hydration Affects Hair Health Hair hydration plays an important role in maintaining soft, smooth, and manageable hair. Adequate moisture levels help maintain hair flexibility and elasticity, while an intact cuticle helps reduce excessive moisture loss. When the cuticle becomes damaged, hair loses moisture more easily, making strands appear dull, brittle, and harder to manage. Hair hydration is influenced by both internal and external factors. Protecting the hair from damage and following appropriate hair care practices can help preserve moisture balance and improve the overall appearance of the hair. Understanding this relationship makes it easier to choose products and routines that suit your hair's needs. Why Hydration Matters for Hair and Scalp Proper moisture balance helps maintain healthy-looking hair and scalp comfort by supporting hair flexibility and the scalp barrier. When moisture levels decline or the cuticle becomes damaged, hair may feel rough, appear dull, and become more prone to breakage. A healthy scalp barrier helps maintain moisture balance and reduce irritation or dryness. However, persistent itching, flaking, or irritation may indicate an underlying scalp condition that requires appropriate evaluation and treatment. How Hair Retains Moisture The hair shaft relies on a healthy moisture balance to maintain its softness, strength, and flexibility. It consists of three layers: the cuticle, cortex, and medulla. The cuticle is the outermost protective layer that helps regulate moisture exchange, while the cortex contains keratin proteins that provide the hair with its strength, elasticity, and structure. When the cuticle remains smooth and intact, it helps retain moisture within the hair shaft, making hair appear softer, shinier, and easier to manage. Hair constantly gains and loses moisture depending on environmental conditions and daily hair care practices. Heat styling, chemical treatments, excessive sun exposure, frequent washing, harsh shampoos, and low humidity can damage the cuticle, allowing moisture to escape more easily. When hair loses moisture or has reduced moisture retention, it may become dry, rough, dull, and frizzy. Maintaining the integrity of the hair cuticle and protecting it from damage helps preserve moisture balance, supporting smoother, stronger, and healthier-looking hair. How Moisture Loss Affects Hair When the cuticle becomes damaged or raised, hair loses moisture more easily, resulting in roughness, frizz, and reduced elasticity. Reduced moisture can also make hair less flexible, increasing the risk of damage during styling and brushing. Hair shine and strength also depend on adequate moisture levels. A smooth cuticle reflects light evenly, giving hair a healthy shine, while well-hydrated hair is more elastic and better able to withstand everyday styling and brushing. As dehydration progresses, hair may become brittle, porous, and more susceptible to breakage. Continued exposure to heat styling, chemical treatments, ultraviolet (UV) radiation, pollution, and dry environmental conditions can further weaken the hair fibre, making it increasingly difficult to maintain soft, smooth, and resilient hair. Water vs Electrolytes for Hair Health Water and electrolytes both play important roles in maintaining the body's hydration. While water supports overall hydration, electrolytes help regulate fluid balance and support normal cellular processes involved in overall health, including skin barrier function. Water is essential for overall hydration, while electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium help regulate fluid balance and support normal cellular functions. Together, they contribute to a healthy internal environment that supports overall scalp health and normal hair function. How Water Supports Hair and Scalp Health Water is essential for overall health and plays an important role in maintaining a healthy scalp environment. While drinking water does not directly hydrate the hair shaft, adequate hydration supports normal physiological functions that contribute to scalp health and the overall appearance of healthy hair. Maintaining proper hydration also helps preserve the body's fluid balance, which is important for healthy skin, including the scalp. Some of the key ways water supports hair and scalp wellness include: Supports Overall Hydration: Water helps maintain the body's fluid balance, which is essential for normal physiological functions, including those that support scalp health. Promotes Scalp Comfort: Adequate hydration helps reduce the feeling of dryness and tightness, supporting a healthier scalp environment. Supports Normal Nutrient Transport: Water plays an important role in transporting nutrients and supporting physiological processes that help maintain healthy skin and scalp tissues. Adequate water intake is an important part of maintaining overall hydration, but it works best alongside a balanced diet and appropriate hair care practices. Together, these measures help support a healthy scalp and maintain soft, smooth, and healthy-looking hair. Role of Electrolytes in Hair Health Electrolytes are minerals such as sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium that help regulate fluid balance, support nerve and muscle function, and maintain normal cellular activity. While electrolytes do not directly hydrate the hair shaft, they play an important role in maintaining the body's hydration status and supporting physiological processes that contribute to overall scalp health. Some of the key roles of electrolytes in maintaining hydration and normal body functions include: Maintain Fluid Balance: It helps regulate water movement throughout the body, supporting normal hydration. Support Cellular Function: Electrolytes help maintain normal cellular activity throughout the body. Replace Minerals Lost Through Sweat: It helps restore electrolyte balance after prolonged sweating, exercise, or heat exposure. Support Overall Scalp Health: Adequate electrolyte balance contributes to a healthy internal environment that supports scalp health. Electrolytes complement, rather than replace, adequate water intake. Maintaining proper hydration through sufficient water consumption and a balanced diet helps support overall health, including a healthy scalp environment that is conducive to normal hair function. Minerals That Support Hair Health Adequate hydration depends not only on drinking enough water but also on maintaining the right balance of essential minerals. These minerals help regulate fluid balance, support normal cellular function, and contribute to overall health. While they do not directly hydrate the hair shaft, they play important roles in maintaining a healthy scalp environment and supporting normal body functions involved in maintaining healthy skin and hair. Some of the key minerals involved in hydration and overall hair health include: Sodium: It helps regulate fluid balance and maintains the movement of water into and out of cells, particularly during sweating, heat exposure, or dehydration. Potassium: It works alongside sodium to maintain fluid balance and supports normal cellular function throughout the body. Magnesium: It supports hundreds of enzymatic reactions involved in energy production, muscle function, and normal cellular processes. Calcium: It plays an important role in cell signalling and supports normal physiological functions, including those involved in skin and scalp health. Chloride: It works with sodium to maintain fluid balance and acid-base balance, helping support normal hydration. Iron: It supports oxygen transport throughout the body, which is essential for normal hair follicle function . Iron deficiency is a well-recognized cause of diffuse hair shedding. Zinc: It supports normal cell growth, tissue repair, and immune function while helping maintain healthy skin and scalp. A balanced diet that provides these essential minerals, along with adequate water intake, supports overall hydration and normal body functions. Combined with a healthy hair care routine, these lifestyle measures help maintain a healthy scalp environment and support healthy-looking hair. Signs of Dry and Dehydrated Hair Water is essential for overall hydration, but healthy-looking hair also depends on its ability to retain moisture. When the hair cuticle becomes damaged or moisture is lost too quickly, the hair may show visible signs of dryness and damage. Recognizing these early changes can help you adjust your hair care routine before the condition worsens. Some common signs that your hair may need additional moisture and nourishment include: Hair Feels Dry After Washing: It may indicate that the hair is unable to retain moisture effectively. Frizz Develops Easily: This can occur when the hair cuticle becomes raised or damaged. Hair Appears Dull: A rough cuticle reflects less light, reducing the hair's natural shine. Hair Breaks Easily: Reduced moisture and elasticity can make strands more prone to breakage. Split Ends Become More Noticeable: Persistent dryness and everyday wear can weaken the ends of the hair. Scalp Feels Dry or Tight: This may suggest scalp dryness, barrier disruption, or irritation. Hair Tangles Frequently: A rougher cuticle increases friction between strands, making hair harder to detangle. Curls Lose Definition: Curly and textured hair naturally loses moisture more easily and may become less defined when dehydrated. Identifying these signs early allows you to take appropriate steps to improve moisture retention and support healthier-looking hair. How Poor Hydration Affects Hair Poor hydration gradually affects both the appearance and behaviour of hair. As moisture levels decline, the cuticle becomes less smooth, reducing elasticity and making strands more prone to tangling and breakage. Curly and textured hair may also lose definition because they naturally struggle to retain moisture. The scalp may also feel dry, tight, or mildly flaky when moisture balance is disrupted or when an underlying scalp condition is present. Recognizing these early changes can help you adjust your hair care routine before dryness leads to further damage. Factors That Affect Hair Hydration Daily habits and environmental conditions can influence the body's hydration status, which also affects scalp health. Factors such as inadequate water intake, poor nutrition, insufficient sleep, prolonged stress, and excessive alcohol consumption can contribute to dehydration. Environmental factors, including hot weather, low humidity, air conditioning, pollution, and ultraviolet (UV) exposure, can also increase moisture loss from the hair. In contrast, high humidity may cause hair, particularly curly or porous hair, to absorb excess moisture from the air, making it more difficult to manage. Physical activity further increases the body's need for hydration. During exercise, water and electrolytes are lost through sweat, particularly sodium and potassium. Replacing these losses by drinking adequate water and following a balanced diet helps maintain normal fluid balance. For people who exercise regularly or spend long periods outdoors, protecting the hair from excessive heat and limiting unnecessary washing can also help minimise moisture loss. Common Hair Hydration Myths Many misconceptions about hair hydration can make it difficult to choose the right hair care routine. While water plays an important role in overall hydration, healthy-looking hair depends on several factors, including moisture retention, scalp health, and protecting the hair from damage. Understanding the facts behind these common myths can help you make informed decisions for healthier hair and scalp. Myth: Water alone is enough to keep hair hydrated. Fact: Water temporarily moisturizes the hair, but it does not stay within the hair shaft for long. Maintaining hydration depends on the hair's ability to retain moisture, which is influenced by the condition of the cuticle and an appropriate hair care routine. Myth: Drinking more water instantly fixes dry hair. Fact: Drinking enough water supports overall hydration and scalp health, but dry hair can also result from heat styling, chemical treatments, environmental exposure, and damage to the hair cuticle. Myth: An oily scalp means your hair is well hydrated. Fact: Oil and hydration are not the same. The scalp may produce excess sebum while the hair shaft remains dry, rough, or prone to breakage. Myth: Electrolytes are only important for athletes. Fact: Electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, and magnesium help regulate fluid balance and normal cellular function in everyone. They become especially important during prolonged sweating, hot weather, illness, or dehydration. Myth: Hydrating hair products always make hair greasy. Fact: Hydrating products are available in different formulations. Choosing products that suit your hair type can help improve moisture levels without making the hair feel heavy or greasy. Myth: Frizzy hair only needs hair oil. Fact: Hair oils help reduce moisture loss by forming a protective layer around the hair shaft, but they do not add moisture. Managing frizz often requires improving moisture retention while protecting the hair from further damage. Understanding these common myths can help you make better hair care decisions and set realistic expectations about hair hydration. A combination of adequate hydration, a balanced diet, appropriate hair care practices, and protection from daily damage can help maintain a healthy scalp and healthier-looking hair. Hydration Routine for Healthy Hair A consistent hydration-focused hair care routine helps maintain moisture balance, improve manageability, and reduce the risk of dryness and breakage. While drinking enough water supports overall hydration, maintaining healthy-looking hair also requires protecting the hair shaft from moisture loss and following a routine suited to your hair type and lifestyle. Some practical steps to build an effective hydration-focused routine include: Use a Gentle Hydrating Shampoo: Choose a mild shampoo such as Wella Professionals Elements Gentle Shampoo , that removes dirt, excess oil, and product buildup without stripping the hair of its natural moisture. Condition After Every Wash: Apply a nourishing conditioner such as Schwarzkopf Professional Spa Essence Conditioner after shampooing to smooth the hair cuticle, reduce tangles, and improve softness and manageability. Deep Condition Weekly: Use a nourishing hair mask such as CITTA Deep Conditioning Hair Mask or deep-conditioning treatment once or twice a week, especially if your hair is dry, damaged, colour-treated, or chemically processed. Apply Leave-in Hydration: Leave-in conditioners such as KERA BOND New Mom's Care Leave-In Hair Conditioner or lightweight hair serums such as Purehill Hair Softening Serum can help improve moisture retention, reduce frizz, and make hair easier to manage between washes. Look for Hydrating Ingredients: Ingredients such as glycerin, panthenol , aloe vera, ceramides, and conditioning agents can help improve moisture retention and hair feel. Maintain Scalp Health: Keep the scalp clean and well cared for by using gentle cleansing products and avoiding excessive product buildup, which can affect overall scalp comfort. Limit Heat Styling: Frequent use of blow dryers, straighteners, and curling tools can increase moisture loss and damage the hair cuticle. When using heat styling tools, apply a heat protectant. Protect Hair from Environmental Damage: Prolonged exposure to sunlight, pollution, wind, and chlorinated water can contribute to dryness. Wearing a hat or using protective hair products may help minimise damage. Stay Adequately Hydrated: Maintaining adequate hydration supports overall health and scalp function, although drinking extra water does not directly increase moisture levels inside the hair shaft. Replenish Electrolytes When Needed: During prolonged exercise, hot weather, or excessive sweating, replacing lost electrolytes through a balanced diet or appropriate rehydration strategies helps maintain normal fluid balance. Avoid Overwashing: Washing hair too frequently may remove natural oils that help protect the hair shaft, particularly in people with dry or curly hair. Adjust Your Routine to Your Hair Type: Fine, curly, coily, colour-treated, or damaged hair has different hydration needs. Choosing products and routines that match your hair type can improve long-term results. Following a consistent routine is more effective than relying on occasional treatments. Combining healthy hydration habits with appropriate hair care practices can help maintain a healthy scalp, improve hair manageability, and support softer, smoother, and healthier-looking hair over time. Nutrition Tips for Healthy Hair Healthy hair moisture depends not only on external hair care but also on daily lifestyle habits and good nutrition. A balanced diet, adequate hydration, and healthy routines help support normal body functions, including those involved in maintaining a healthy scalp and healthy-looking hair. While these habits do not directly hydrate the hair shaft, they contribute to the overall environment needed for healthy hair. Some daily habits that support healthy hair moisture include: Drink Adequate Water: Drinking enough water helps maintain overall hydration and supports normal physiological functions that contribute to scalp health. Eat Electrolyte-Rich Foods: It is beneficial to include foods such as fruits, vegetables, dairy products, nuts, and seeds, which provide minerals like potassium, magnesium, and calcium that help maintain fluid balance. Include Healthy Fats: It is important to consume healthy fats from foods such as walnuts, flaxseeds, chia seeds, and oily fish, as they support overall skin and scalp health. Consume Enough Protein: Hair is primarily composed of keratin, a structural protein. Eating adequate protein helps support normal hair growth and maintain hair strength. Follow a Nutrient-Rich Diet: Adequate intake of nutrients such as iron, zinc, vitamin D, and protein supports normal hair growth, particularly when deficiencies are present. Limit Excessive Alcohol Consumption: Excessive alcohol intake can contribute to dehydration, making it important to maintain adequate fluid intake as part of a healthy lifestyle. Prioritize Good Sleep and Stress Management: Healthy sleep habits and stress management support overall well-being and may help maintain a healthier scalp environment. Internal Hydration and Hair Care Healthy hair benefits from combining good hydration habits with consistent topical care. While drinking enough water and eating a balanced diet support overall hydration, conditioners , leave-in treatments, and other moisturizing products help protect the hair cuticle and minimise moisture loss caused by everyday styling and environmental exposure. Combining internal hydration with an appropriate hair care routine provides a more complete approach to maintaining soft, manageable, and healthy-looking hair. When to See a Dermatologist for Dry Hair Occasional hair dryness is common and often improves with appropriate hair care and lifestyle changes. However, if dryness persists despite following a consistent hydration-focused routine, it may indicate an underlying scalp condition, nutritional deficiency, hair shaft disorder, or another health concern. Seeking professional advice can help identify the underlying cause and ensure you receive appropriate treatment. You should consider consulting a dermatologist if you notice any of the following: Persistent Dryness Despite Routine Care: If your hair remains dry even after using suitable shampoos, conditioners, and other moisturizing products, a professional evaluation may help identify the underlying cause. Excessive Hair Breakage: If your hair becomes increasingly brittle, develops frequent split ends, or breaks easily during normal brushing or styling, it may require further assessment. Ongoing Scalp Dryness or Irritation: Persistent itching, flaking, redness, or scalp discomfort may indicate an underlying scalp condition rather than simple dryness. Sudden Changes in Hair Texture: If your hair becomes noticeably rough, dull, or difficult to manage without an obvious cause, it is worth discussing these changes with a healthcare professional. Hair Dryness With Excessive Hair Loss: Dryness accompanied by increased hair shedding or thinning may be associated with nutritional deficiencies, hormonal changes, or certain scalp disorders that require evaluation. Damage Following Chemical Treatments: Hair that becomes severely dry or fragile after colouring, bleaching, straightening, or perming may benefit from professional guidance on repairing and protecting the hair. Recurring Hair or Scalp Concerns: If dryness, frizz, scalp irritation, or other symptoms continue to return despite appropriate care, a dermatologist can help determine the underlying cause and recommend a personalised treatment plan. Persistent hair dryness does not always indicate a serious problem, but recurring or worsening symptoms should not be ignored. A dermatologist can evaluate your hair and scalp, identify contributing factors, and recommend evidence-based treatments and hair care practices based on your individual needs. Final Thoughts Healthy hair hydration involves more than simply drinking enough water. Maintaining soft, smooth, and healthy-looking hair also depends on the hair's ability to retain moisture. Factors such as hair type, climate, daily habits, and hair care practices all influence how well your hair stays hydrated over time. A balanced approach that combines adequate hydration, good nutrition, and a consistent hair care routine can help support healthier-looking hair and scalp. If persistent dryness, breakage, or scalp discomfort continues despite proper care, consult a dermatologist to identify any underlying cause and receive appropriate treatment.

title: How to Create a Restaurant Menu
summary: How to create a restaurant menu that drives orders: profit-first ordering, sharper descriptions, price formatting, and the photo data behind a 44% lift.
body_text: A menu is a pricing document wearing a costume Forty dishes, one afternoon, zero gaps. DoorDash puts full coverage at up to 44% more sales. Every guest reads it. Nobody trains it. It works every shift you're open. That matters more in 2026 than it did five years ago, because margin has nowhere left to hide. The National Restaurant Association reports that 42% of operators said their restaurant was not profitable last year, and 60% reported softer customer traffic. You can't fix that with a price increase alone. You can fix a meaningful slice of it by changing what your menu asks people to buy. Here's how to build one that does the work. Step 1: Rank items by contribution, not by popularity The menu makes a promise. The plate has to keep it, or the refunds start. Most operators build a menu around what sells. Build it around what sells and earns. Pull ninety days of sales data and calculate contribution margin per item, which is menu price minus food cost. Then plot every item on two axes: how often it sells, and how much it contributes. High-margin, high-volume items are your leads. They belong in the top-right of a printed page and in the first two rows of a digital menu. Low-margin, low-volume items are the ones to cut. A shorter menu is a faster kitchen, less waste, and a guest who decides in twenty seconds instead of two minutes. Step 2: Write descriptions that carry weight Uber Eats says item descriptions and photos can boost menu conversion by up to 50%, and descriptions are the cheaper half of that pair. Good ones are short and specific. Name the technique, the origin, or the one ingredient that makes the dish itself. "Slow-braised beef short rib, black garlic, charred spring onion" tells a guest what they're getting. "Delicious short rib with vegetables" tells them nothing and gets skipped. Skip adjectives that could describe any dish on any menu. Fresh, tasty and mouth-watering are filler. Cut them and you'll find room for a real detail. Step 3: Take the dollar signs off your prices This one is nearly free. Cornell researchers gave 201 diners at a Culinary Institute of America café one of three menus: prices with dollar signs, prices as bare numerals, or prices written out in words. Guests reading the numeral-only menu spent an average of $5.55 more, roughly 8%, than the other two groups. A dollar sign is a small reminder of the pain of paying. Remove it and you remove the reminder. Format prices as 24 rather than $24.00, drop the trailing cents, and never run a row of dots leading the eye from the dish straight to the number. Step 4: Photograph every item, not just the hero dishes Nobody reaches for a dish they can't picture. Uber Eats: photos plus copy, up to 50% more. Photo coverage is the single largest lever in this list. DoorDash analyzed over 15,000 local small business merchants and found menus with item photos get up to 44% more monthly sales. Coverage is what matters. An item without a photo sitting next to eight items that have one reads as an afterthought, and guests order around it. We've written before about the image gaps that quietly cost restaurants orders on delivery apps , and the pattern is consistent: partial coverage suppresses the uncovered items rather than lifting the covered ones. Shoot every dish the same way. Same angle family, same light direction, same surface, same distance from the plate. Consistency is what makes a set of photos read as a menu instead of a camera roll. Our guide to choosing the right menu photographer covers what to look for if you're hiring out. Step 5: Build for the phone, then print Your digital menu is the one most guests see first. Design it there, then adapt the print version, not the other way around. That means: categories a thumb can reach, no more than seven items per category, photos cropped square, and descriptions that survive being truncated at two lines. Our walkthrough on creating a visually strong online menu goes deeper on layout. The part that stalls most operators Nobody struggles with the theory. They struggle with photographing forty items, then re-photographing the six they change next quarter, then doing it again when they open a second location. That's the job Snappr does. You book a vetted food photographer in about two minutes with as little as 24 hours' notice, define your shoot guidelines once so every future shoot matches the first, and get edited images back in 24 to 48 hours. When a dish changes, you rebook a single item rather than restaging the whole menu. Explore Snappr for menus and restaurants to see how it works across one location or fifty. Frequently asked questions How many items should a restaurant menu have? Most independent restaurants perform best with 20 to 40 items across all categories, with no more than seven items per category. Longer menus slow decisions, increase food waste, and dilute the items that actually carry your margin. How often should you update a restaurant menu? Review pricing and item mix quarterly, and refresh the full menu once or twice a year. Update photos any time a dish's plating, portion, or garnish changes, because a photo that no longer matches the plate creates refunds and bad reviews. Do menu photos really increase sales? Yes. DoorDash's study of more than 15,000 small business merchants found menus with item photos get up to 44% more monthly sales, and Uber Eats reports descriptions and photos together can lift conversion by up to 50%. Should you put dollar signs on a restaurant menu? The Cornell research suggests not. Diners given a numeral-only menu spent about 8% more per person than those given menus with dollar signs or written-out prices. What is the best way to organize menu categories? Order categories the way people eat, then order items within each category by contribution margin. Put your highest-earning, highest-selling dish first in its category, because the first item in a list gets disproportionate attention. Sources 1. DoorDash Merchant Blog, menu photography — study of 15,000+ small business merchants, 44% more monthly sales from item photos 3. Uber Eats, menu descriptions — descriptions and photos boosting menu conversion by up to 50% 4. Cornell Chronicle, 2009 — Yang, Kimes and Sessarego study of 201 diners, $5.55 higher spend without dollar signs

body_text: For decades, the debate surrounding vaccines and autism has resurfaced despite overwhelming scientific evidence rejecting any connection. The discussion has returned to the spotlight after President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. raised questions about vaccine safety, even as a major new study involving more than 2.5 million American children once again found no evidence that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine causes autism. The latest research adds to one of the largest bodies of evidence in modern medicine, reinforcing findings from health organizations and scientists worldwide. It also arrives during a challenging period for public health in the United States, where childhood vaccination rates have declined and measles cases have surged to their highest level in more than three decades. Large Study Finds No Association Between MMR Vaccine and Autism A newly published study involving over 2.5 million children in the United States found that receiving the MMR vaccine before the age of two does not increase the likelihood of an autism diagnosis. Researchers from the University of Washington concluded that their findings reinforce decades of scientific evidence supporting the vaccine's safety. According to the research team, the results strengthen confidence in childhood immunization programs and align with previous studies conducted across multiple countries over several decades. Similar conclusions have also been reached by the World Health Organization and numerous independent scientific organizations. The findings are particularly significant because the study analyzed one of the largest groups of children ever examined for this question, making the evidence even more robust. Why the Debate Has Returned The renewed attention comes after recent comments from President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who have suggested that more investigation into possible vaccine related causes of autism is warranted. Trump has previously expressed concerns about the combined MMR vaccine, suggesting it should be administered as separate vaccines rather than as a single shot. He has also questioned ingredients such as mercury and aluminum, although the standard MMR vaccine does not contain mercury based preservatives. Meanwhile, Kennedy acknowledged during a television interview that people should receive the MMR vaccine for protection against measles. However, he also questioned whether previous research into vaccines and autism has been sufficient, despite decades of published studies reaching the same conclusion. These statements have sparked renewed public discussion, especially as the United States continues to battle increasing measles outbreaks. Measles Cases Continue to Rise Public health officials are increasingly concerned about falling vaccination rates. Federal data shows that MMR vaccination coverage among children has gradually declined since before the COVID-19 pandemic. At the same time, measles infections have climbed sharply, reaching the highest levels seen in approximately 35 years. Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known. It can lead to severe complications including pneumonia, brain inflammation, permanent disability, and death, particularly among infants and individuals with weakened immune systems. Health experts emphasize that maintaining high vaccination coverage is essential to prevent widespread outbreaks. The Origin of the Autism Myth The belief that the MMR vaccine causes autism can largely be traced back to a 1998 paper published by former British physician Andrew Wakefield. The study involved only a small number of children and claimed there might be a connection between the MMR vaccine and developmental disorders. However, investigators later uncovered serious methodological flaws, ethical violations, and undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. The journal that published the research fully retracted the paper, and Wakefield eventually lost his medical license. Despite being thoroughly discredited, the study received significant media attention and continues to influence public opinion decades later. Medical experts frequently cite the Wakefield case as one of the most prominent examples of how misinformation can spread rapidly and remain influential long after it has been disproven. What Scientific Research Shows Since the original controversy emerged, researchers across the world have conducted numerous large scale studies examining whether vaccines contribute to autism spectrum disorder. These investigations have included millions of children from different countries, healthcare systems, and demographic groups. The consistent conclusion has remained unchanged. Researchers have found no evidence that receiving the MMR vaccine increases autism risk. Scientists also note that autism symptoms often become noticeable around the same age children receive routine vaccinations. This timing can create the false impression that one event caused the other, even though scientific evidence does not support a causal relationship. CDC Changes Spark Debate The discussion has also intensified following updates to information published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The agency revised language on its website regarding vaccines and autism, stating that investigations into possible biological mechanisms and potential causal links remain part of a broader assessment into autism. The revised wording has drawn criticism from several medical organizations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, which argues that reopening questions already addressed through extensive scientific research risks spreading unnecessary confusion. Health experts warn that uncertainty surrounding vaccine safety may contribute to declining immunization rates and increased vulnerability to preventable diseases. Why Vaccination Still Matters Medical professionals continue to recommend routine childhood vaccinations because of their proven ability to prevent serious infectious diseases. Before widespread vaccination, measles caused millions of infections worldwide every year and led to hundreds of thousands of deaths annually. The MMR vaccine has dramatically reduced those numbers in countries with strong vaccination programs. Health authorities stress that vaccination not only protects the individual receiving the shot but also helps safeguard infants, elderly individuals, cancer patients, and others who may not be able to receive vaccines themselves. Final Thoughts The latest study involving more than 2.5 million American children further strengthens decades of scientific evidence showing that the MMR vaccine does not cause autism. While public debate continues and political figures call for additional investigations, the current body of medical research remains remarkably consistent. Independent studies conducted around the world have repeatedly found no causal link between the MMR vaccine and autism. At a time when measles cases are rising and vaccination rates are falling, health experts continue to emphasize that maintaining confidence in evidence based immunization programs remains one of the most effective ways to protect public health. Source: The Independent and supported by publicly available scientific findings from the University of Washington study, the World Health Organization (WHO), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), and FactCheck.org. Readers should consult qualified healthcare professionals or official public health authorities regarding vaccination decisions or medical concerns.

body_text: View All News Driven Brands Holdings Inc. Rejects Non-Binding, Highly Conditional and Unsolicited Proposal from ADW Capital August 3, 2026 Proposal Significantly Undervalues the Company and Is Not in the Best Interest of Driven Brands and its Shareholders CHARLOTTE, N.C.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Driven Brands Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ: DRVN) (“Driven Brands” or the “Company”), North America's largest automotive services company, today announced that its Board of Directors has unanimously rejected ADW Capital Management, LLC’s (“ADW Capital”) non-binding, highly conditional and unsolicited proposal to acquire Driven Brands for $18.00 per share in cash. Consistent with its fiduciary duties and in consultation with its financial and legal advisors, the Board carefully reviewed and evaluated ADW Capital’s proposal. Following its review, the Driven Brands Board unanimously determined that ADW Capital’s proposal is highly conditional and does not provide a credible basis on which the Company could proceed. Additionally, the Board concluded that ADW Capital’s proposal significantly undervalues the Company in light of its long-term value creation opportunities and is therefore not in the best interest of Driven Brands and its shareholders. The Driven Brands Board and leadership team remain confident in the Company’s strategy, long-term value creation opportunities and disciplined execution. The Board remains committed to acting in the best interests of all shareholders and to evaluating opportunities to maximize shareholder value. About Driven Brands Driven Brands™, headquartered in Charlotte, NC, is the largest automotive services company in North America, providing a range of consumer and commercial automotive services, including oil change, paint, collision, glass, vehicle repair, and maintenance. Driven Brands is the parent company of some of North America’s leading automotive service businesses including Take 5 Oil Change®, Meineke Car Care Centers®, Maaco®, 1-800-Radiator & A/C®, Auto Glass Now®, and CARSTAR®. As of the end of fiscal year 2025, Driven Brands had over 4,200 locations across the U.S. and Canada, and services tens of millions of vehicles annually. Driven Brands’ network generated approximately $1.9 billion in annual revenue from approximately $6.1 billion in system-wide sales. title: Indivior Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Raises Full-Year 2026 Guidance
summary: • Q2’26 Total Net Revenue of $ 343 Million, Up 14% YoY • Record Quarterly Total SUBLOCADE® Net Revenue of $ 253 Million in Q2'26, Up 21% YoY • Record Quarterly GAAP Net Income of $122 Million and Record Non-GAAP Net Income of $142 Million in Q2'26 • Record Quarterly Adjusted EBITDA of $ 186
body_text: Indivior Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Raises Full-Year 2026 Guidance August 3, 2026 PDF Version • Q2’26 Total Net Revenue of $ 343 Million, Up 14% YoY • Record Quarterly Total SUBLOCADE® Net Revenue of $ 253 Million in Q2'26, Up 21% YoY • Record Quarterly GAAP Net Income of $122 Million and Record Non-GAAP Net Income of $142 Million in Q2'26 • Record Quarterly Adjusted EBITDA of $ 186 Million in Q2'26, Up 111% YoY • Repurchased Approximately 4.7 Million Shares in Q2'26 for $175 Million RICHMOND, Va., Aug. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Indivior Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Nasdaq: INDV) today reported its financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, and raised its full-year 2026 financial guidance. “Exceptional operational execution in Phase II – Accelerate – of the Indivior Action Agenda fueled strong SUBLOCADE performance in the quarter and is the primary driver of our raised 2026 guidance,” said Joe Ciaffoni, Chief Executive Officer. "We remain focused on Phase II – Accelerate – for the remainder of 2026 and look forward to closing our proposed merger with Supernus, which is expected in the fourth quarter. Upon the close of our proposed merger, all three Phases of the Indivior Action Agenda will have been successfully completed.” “We delivered record SUBLOCADE net revenue and adjusted EBITDA in the quarter leading us to raise our 2026 guidance,” said Ryan Preblick, Chief Financial Officer. "We now expect 2026 total SUBLOCADE net revenue growth of 20% year-over-year and adjusted EBITDA growth of 68% year-over-year at the midpoint of our guidance ranges. We returned capital to our shareholders through the repurchase of $175 million in shares during the quarter. We are committed to creating long-term shareholder value.” Q2 2026 Business Highlights : As of June 30, 2026, over 545,000 patients in the U.S. have been prescribed SUBLOCADE since launch. Grew total SUBLOCADE net revenue 21% year-over-year to $253 million. U.S. SUBLOCADE net revenue increased 22% year-over-year to $238 million versus the prior year, driven by 18% dispense unit volume growth. New patient starts of 32,816 were a record. Net revenue also benefited from more favorable price/mix and gross-to-net adjustments. In the second quarter, Indivior repurchased 4,664,540 shares at an average price of $37.52 for a total of $175 million. Year-to-date, the Company has repurchased 8,638,693 shares at an average price of $34.73 for a total of $300 million. Announced findings from two new real-world evidence studies showing that adherence to SUBLOCADE is associated with lower relapse risk, fewer infection-related complications, and reduced healthcare utilization among people living with opioid use disorder (OUD). Indivior Pharmaceuticals, Inc. and Supernus Pharmaceuticals, Inc. today announced a definitive agreement to combine in an all-stock merger of equals transaction to create a leading, diversified, scaled, CNS-focused biopharmaceutical company. For additional information on the transaction, please reference the announcement press release at Indivior.com . Raising Full-Year 2026 Financial Guidance : Full-year financial guidance assumes no material change in exchange rates for key currencies compared with 2025 average rates, notably USD/GBP and USD/EUR. Accordingly, the Company has relied upon the exception in Item 10(e)(1)(i)(B) of Regulation S-K to exclude such reconciliations, as the reconciliations of these non-U.S. GAAP guidance metrics to their corresponding U.S. GAAP equivalents are not available without unreasonable effort. Financial Results for Quarter Ended June 30, 2026 : Total net revenue was $343 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 (the 2026 quarter), compared to $302 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2025 (the 2025 quarter), representing a 14% increase year-over-year. Total SUBLOCADE net revenue was $253 million for the 2026 quarter, compared to $209 million for the 2025 quarter, representing a 21% increase year-over-year. GAAP operating expenses were $134 million for the 2026 quarter, compared to $179 million for the 2025 quarter, representing a 25% decrease year-over-year. Non-GAAP operating expenses, which exclude stock-based compensation expense and other adjustments to reflect changes that occur in our business but do not represent ongoing operations, were $112 million for the 2026 quarter, compared to $167 million for the 2025 quarter, representing a 33% decrease year-over-year. GAAP net income for the 2026 quarter was $122 million ($0.98 diluted earnings per share), compared to GAAP net income for the 2025 quarter of $18 million ($0.14 diluted earnings per share). Non-GAAP net income for the 2026 quarter was $142 million ($1.15 diluted earnings per share), compared to non-GAAP net income for the 2025 quarter of $64 million ($0.51 diluted earnings per share). Adjusted EBITDA for the 2026 quarter was $186 million, compared to $88 million for the 2025 quarter, representing a 111% increase year-over-year. The Company ended the 2026 quarter with cash and investments of $249 million. Financial Results for Six Months Ended June 30, 2026 : Total net revenue was $660 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026 (the 2026 period), compared to $568 million for the six months ended June 30, 2025 (the 2025 period), representing a 16% increase year-over-year. Total SUBLOCADE net revenue was $486 million for the 2026 period, compared to $385 million for the 2025 period, representing a 26% increase year-over-year. GAAP operating expenses were $273 million for the 2026 period, compared to $334 million for the 2025 period, representing an 18% decrease year-over-year. Non-GAAP operating expenses, which exclude stock-based compensation expense and other adjustments to reflect changes that occur in our business but do not represent ongoing operations, were $229 million for the 2026 period, compared to $313 million for the 2025 period, representing a 27% decrease year-over-year. GAAP net income for the 2026 period was $211 million ($1.67 diluted earnings per share), compared to GAAP net income for the 2025 period of $65 million ($0.52 diluted earnings per share). Non-GAAP net income for the 2026 period was $266 million ($2.10 diluted earnings per share), compared to non-GAAP net income for the 2025 period of $121 million ($0.96 diluted earnings per share). Adjusted EBITDA for the 2026 period was $350 million, compared to $165 million for the 2025 period, representing a 112% increase year-over-year. Conference Call and Webcast Details : As a result of the transaction announcement today, Indivior will host a joint transaction conference call with Supernus in lieu of its previously scheduled second quarter 2026 earnings conference call. A live webcast will be available here or from the Investor Relations section of both companies’ website at Supernus Events & Presentations and www.indivior.com . Participants may also pre-register any time before the call here . Once registration is completed, participants will be provided a dial-in number with a personalized conference code to access the call. Please dial in 15 minutes prior to the start time. A replay of the webcast will be available following the event. An investor presentation, which will be referenced during the webcast, is also available from the Investor Relations section of both companies' websites. About Indivior As the leader in long-acting injectable treatments for opioid use disorder (OUD), Indivior is singularly focused on delivering evidence-based treatment and advancing understanding of OUD as a chronic but treatable brain disease. For more than 25 years, we have revolutionized the science of addiction medicine — developing treatments that help people move toward long-term recovery with independence and dignity. Building on this heritage, we are ushering in a new era, renewing our commitment to individuals living with OUD and carrying forward what matters most: compassion, integrity, and science. Together – with science, people living with OUD, public health champions, and communities, we are powering recovery and renewing hope. Visit www.indivior.com to learn more.
