Age Verification Tools: How They Work and Who Needs Them
summary: Age verification tools help businesses comply with regulations on selling age-restricted products online like alcohol and tobacco. Learn how they work.
body_text: This post is for information only. You are responsible for reviewing and using this information appropriately. This content doesn’t contain and isn’t meant to provide legal, tax, or business advice. Requirements are updated frequently and you should make sure to do your own research and reach out to professional legal, tax, and business advisers, as needed. To sell products using the Shopify platform, you must comply with the laws of the jurisdiction of your business and your customers, the Shopify Terms of Service, the Shopify Acceptable Use Policy, and any other applicable policies. Age verification tools are software solutions that confirm a customer’s age before completing a sale of age-restricted products. They range in sophistication from simple self-declaration pop-ups to AI-powered facial age estimation and full document verification systems that check government-issued IDs in real time. For stores selling anything with a legally mandated minimum purchase age—vaping products, alcoholic beverages, or certain dietary supplements—simply asking visitors to click a button declaring they’re over the legal age no longer satisfies many lawmakers and regulators. In the US, rules vary by state and product category. Overseas, some countries have more cohesive, nationwide and industry-neutral age-verification laws. The UK’s Office of Communications (Ofcom), for instance, does not count self-declaration as a “highly effective” method of age assurance under the 2023 Online Safety Act . This guide covers what age verification tools are, how they work, the legal and regulatory requirements that prompt them, and which age verification software and services fit different store setups. What are age verification tools? Age verification tools are software products that confirm whether a customer meets the minimum age requirements to purchase or access age-restricted goods or age-restricted content. In ecommerce, these tools typically live on the landing page, product page, or checkout page to block underage users before a transaction is completed or to record that an age check has occurred. Age gates vs. true age verification Simple age gates and true age verification are not the same: Age gates. Asks potential customers to confirm their age, usually with a yes or no button or birthdate input field. These selections aren’t verified against any external information. True age verification. Runs the customer’s information against an independent source such as a government database, an ID document scan, a credit card check, or facial recognition technology. While some states only require age gates, others have stringent requirements for age verification. For example, Louisiana requires ID verification for some age-restricted products sold online. If you sell to customers in Louisiana, you’re obligated to meet these requirements, even if you’re based in another state. Types of age verification methods ID document verification Database checks Facial age estimation Credit card verification Digital ID wallets Self-declaration Age verification methods vary in the tradeoffs they make between friction, accuracy, and privacy. Some of the more common age verification methods include the following. ID document verification ID document verification requires a customer to photograph their government-issued identification, like a passport or driver’s license, with their device camera. It’s a highly accurate verification process because it checks against a real government-issued credential. The trade-off is that this method asks a lot of customers. Uploading a photo of an ID mid-checkout is a meaningful barrier. According to the Baymard Institute , 18% of customers have abandoned an online purchase because the checkout process was too long or complicated. ID verification is best suited to high-compliance industries, like selling wine online , where regulatory requirements demand a verified identity rather than just a plausible one. ID document verification also produces a clear audit trail, useful if your business ever needs to prove age check compliance to a regulator. Database checks Database checks use the name, address, and date of birth a customer enters at checkout to verify their age—there’s no upload, redirect, or extra step. The limitation here is that accuracy depends on the quality of the identity data infrastructure in a given market. In the US, where commercial identity databases and public records data are relatively robust, database checks typically return a pass-fail result within seconds, without requiring customers to upload ID or complete a separate account registration. In markets with less developed databases, match rates drop and more customers end up being flagged for manual review or secondary verification. Because these checks often involve sharing customers’ personal information with a third-party verification provider, ensure your data handling practices comply with applicable privacy laws and are accurately reflected in privacy disclosures. Important regulations to be aware of, given the number of potential online customers covered by them, include the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA ), the Texas Data Privacy and Security Act , the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) , and the UK’s General Data Protection Regulation . Facial age estimation Facial age estimation uses artificial intelligence (AI) to estimate a customer’s age from a photo of their face—typically without storing any identity data, only a pass-or-fail result, though data retention practices may vary by provider. Because face recognition is a probabilistic process, it can work better as a threshold filter (clearly over 18, clearly under 18) than as a precise confirmation. It serves businesses that need to demonstrate they’ve taken reasonable steps to screen out minors, especially in markets like the UK where “highly effective age assurance” methods, like facial age estimation, are explicitly recognized as compliant under the Online Safety Act. It’s less suitable where regulations require confirmed age verification rather than an estimate. Credit card verification Credit card verification infers age from the cardholder record. If the card is linked to an adult’s account, the customer likely meets the minimum age. The catch here is that it confirms the cardholder’s age, but not necessarily the person actually placing the order. For example, a teenager using a parent’s card might pass. For this reason, this method is unlikely to satisfy regulatory scrutiny for the most strictly regulated goods, such as nicotine products, alcohol, gambling services, and legal cannabis. Digital ID wallets Digital ID wallets let customers present a verified digital credential from a national identity system, sharing only a pass-or-fail result (such as “over 18”) without handing over personal data like their exact age. It’s a privacy-preserving form of confirmed verification, but it’s still emerging and only available in jurisdictions where there are established government-approved digital identity programs. The approach is gaining ground: Countries including Estonia and Singapore already run national digital identity systems, and in July 2025 the EU released a blueprint—built on the same framework as the forthcoming EU Digital Identity Wallet—to support the Digital Services Act ’s rules on protecting minors online. Self-declaration Self-declaration is a simple yes-or-no button or birthdate entry field. It creates a digital log showing the customer acknowledged an age requirement. While self-declaration creates a record of acknowledgement, it is not a form of true age verification, and many age verification laws, for example in Canada and the UK , now explicitly exclude it as a compliant method. Some sellers use self-declaration as an initial age gate when a visitor arrives on the site, then apply a separate age verification method at checkout before completing a purchase. Work smarter with apps Expand your store features with more than 8,000 apps from the Shopify App Store. Find everything from dropshipping suppliers to AI-powered customer support and additional apps to help you do more. Browse apps Top age verification tools BlueCheck AgeChecker.net Token of Trust Yoti NA Age Verification The right tool for your online store depends on the specific combination of compliance requirements you need to meet. Other considerations include the amount of friction you’re willing to introduce into the checkout process, how technically complex your website is, and what integration options your ecommerce platform supports. These tools are designed to slot into existing systems at checkout with minimal development work—making them useful for stores without dedicated technical resources. BlueCheck BlueCheck runs age verification silently during checkout, matching customer information against commercial identity databases without disrupting the purchase flow. It mainly uses database checks, with fallback options like a photo, scan of a government ID, or the last four digits of a US Social Security number (SSN) for customers who can’t be automatically confirmed. Other key features include tailored location-based compliance settings, product-level filtering, and bulk pre-approved user lists. BlueCheck also supports liveness detection, which is a technological security measure that confirms a person is physically present during an identity check, rather than uploading a still image, screenshot, deepfake, or spoofed video, for higher-security document checks and has global coverage across major markets. Pricing starts at $25 a month with 25 verifications included, with additional verifications at $1.25 each. Mid-tier and upper-tier plans run between $100 and $250 a month, with up to 500 verifications included and progressively lower per-verification rates. AgeChecker.net AgeChecker.net verifies age by having customers input their date of birth during the checkout process, and verifies this data along with name and address, against commercial databases. There’s generally no requirement to upload a document or provide any atypical personal data such as the last four digits of an SSN. Customers who fail the automatic check can be prompted for a photo ID as a secondary step, with an optional real-time selfie for strictly regulated products, which can be activated by sellers as an additional layer of compliance. Location-based age rules let you apply different thresholds by state or country to meet jurisdictional requirements. The tool’s dashboard helps you track individual customers’ verification attempts—helpful for identifying holes in the system or potential fraud—and organize audit-ready verification logs. Pricing is based on a flat monthly subscription fee of $25, with 50¢ per accepted verification. Users only pay for verifications that go through. Token of Trust Token of Trust combines database checks, document verification, and facial age estimation. You can tag specific products to trigger age verification, recognize returning customers to fast-track repeat purchases, and support compliance across a wide range of international markets. Verification can be inserted between inputting billing information and actual payment for pre-checkout confirmation. The platform also includes a suite of fraud detection and compliance auditing tools. A basic package with simple document verification and optional database checks and selfie matches starts at $25 a month , plus 85¢ per verification. More advanced plans, ranging from $160 to $250 a month, include built-in fallback procedures for manual review and a suite of know-your-customer (KYC) compliance and anti-money laundering tools. KYC refers to mandatory regulatory standards used by international financial institutions. Yoti Yoti has 10 age verification methods, ranging from a selfie-based AI age estimator to a full passport scan and verified digital ID. It can be a strong fit for businesses that sell globally and need to comply with a variety of consumer privacy laws across different industries and sales channels . Rather than storing customer data locally, Yoti returns only a pass-fail result, reducing overall privacy risk and simplifying compliance with data protection laws like the GDPR. Yoti’s facial age estimation and digital ID methods are also recognized as compliant approaches under the UK Online Safety Act. For non-enterprise individual users—including those integrating via Shopify—Yoti is a free-to-install age verification software provider with no upfront cost. Sitewide age verification before store access, checkout stage verification for specific age-restricted products, customizable age minimum requirements, and geotagging are all free. However, more sophisticated age-verification features and higher volume may require a paid plan. NA Age Verification NA Age Verification is a basic age gate for stores that need a compliant entry barrier rather than a true identity-confirmed age verification. It adds a customizable pop-up at site entry or before checkout, with options for self-declaration through yes or no, check the box, or birthdate input. Features include page-level and order-level targeting—letting sellers place gates only on relevant product pages or carts containing tagged items—plus integration options with third-party apps like Klaviyo. Because this is a self-declaration tool, it’s suitable for lower-risk product categories but not for regulated industries requiring true identity verification. A basic free package is available, with paid tiers ranging from $3.95 to $8.95 per month. Higher tiers add the ability to attach pop-ups to specific pages, customizable branding, checkout disabling until verification, and enhanced audit logging. Shopify features that support age verification Beyond integration of third-party apps, Shopify has built-in features that complement your age verification solutions. Shopify Flow lets you automate workflows based on age verification outcomes—holding or tagging orders that fail a check. For shipments that use Canada Post , Shopify has an option that triggers in-person age verification at the point of delivery for anywhere in Canada (18+ or 19+ thresholds). And Shopify Managed Markets automatically limits age-restricted goods for international sales so orders don’t hang in limbo while someone on your team manually checks and clears the age verification. Age verification tools FAQ What is the easiest way to verify age? Database checks are the lowest friction for customers, running silently in the background using already input checkout information. Self-declaration pop-ups are the simplest to set up, but don’t constitute true age verification under most age verification laws. What is a safe age verification app? A safe age verification app is calibrated to comply with a variety of jurisdictional age verification laws like the GDPR and UK Online Safety Act, stores only the minimum data required, and is transparent about how customer data is handled. What is the best age verification method? There’s no single best method for age verification. The right approach depends on the regulatory requirements where your business is based and where you sell products, product categories in your store, and your customer base. Document verification is the most accurate, facial age estimation has the best privacy preservation, and database checks have the lowest checkout friction for customers in markets with strong identity data infrastructure.

title: What Is Metered Billing? How It Works
summary: Metered billing charges for what customers actually use, measured after the fact. Here's how it works, how it differs from usage-based and subscription billing, and when you need dedicated metering software.
body_text: Metered billing charges customers based on what they actually use: API calls, compute time, storage, tokens, measured and billed after the fact, rather than a fixed price agreed upfront. It's the mechanism underneath usage-based pricing. Usage-based pricing decides what to charge for and how much ; metered billing is what measures usage accurately enough to bill on it. GitHub uses it for Copilot's AI Credits. Stripe ships it as a built-in billing feature. Lago meters usage as event data in real time, at up to one million events per second, so pricing logic runs on usage as it happens instead of in a nightly batch. What is metered billing? Metered billing is a pricing mechanism where a customer's invoice is calculated from measured consumption rather than a pre-agreed flat fee. The bill isn't known in advance. It's the output of tracking usage over a billing period and applying a rate to it, the same way a utility company reads a water or electricity meter before sending an invoice. That's the whole idea. Everything else, usage-based pricing, hybrid plans, overage tiers, is a decision layered on top of the fact that usage was metered in the first place. For how this term sits alongside other billing and pricing vocabulary, see Lago's pricing and billing glossary . How does metered billing work? Metered billing runs on four steps: usage is captured as events, those events are aggregated into a billable metric, a pricing rule is applied to that metric, and the result becomes a line on an invoice. Capture. Every unit of consumption (an API call, a gigabyte stored, a token generated) gets sent as a usage event, typically over an events API as it happens rather than pulled from logs after the fact. At scale, this is a real throughput problem before it's a pricing problem. Lago's ingestion layer is built to handle up to 1,000,000 events per second, because a metering system that can't keep up with usage can't be trusted to bill on it. Deduplicate. Events get retried, duplicated, and sent out of order. A metering system has to treat each event as idempotent, so the same usage doesn't get counted twice and a customer doesn't get billed for something that never happened. Aggregate. Raw events become a billable metric using an aggregation rule. The four common ones: COUNT (how many API calls this month), UNIQUE COUNT (how many distinct active users, not requests), SUM (total GB transferred), and MAX (peak concurrent seats in a billing period, even if usage dropped afterward). Which one you pick changes what the customer is actually paying for: COUNT bills for activity, SUM bills for volume, MAX bills for peak commitment. Rate and invoice. The aggregated metric gets a price applied (a flat per-unit rate, a graduated tier, or a volume discount) and rolls into the invoice at the end of the billing cycle. This whole pipeline is usually driven by a metering API: a product sends events in, the billing platform meters, prices, and invoices them out, without a human touching a spreadsheet in between. This is exactly the shape of the problem for API products billing on usage , where requests, tokens, or bytes are the unit and the metering has to keep pace with production traffic. For the deeper architecture behind this (idempotency keys, aggregation at scale, rating engine design), see the full playbook on architecting usage-based billing systems . Metered billing vs. usage-based billing: what's the difference? Usage-based billing is the pricing strategy: the decision to charge by consumption instead of a flat seat fee. Metered billing is the infrastructure underneath it: the system that actually measures usage accurately enough to bill on. You can't run usage-based pricing without some form of metering, but metering itself is a technical concern, not a pricing decision. Take the same API product priced two ways. Priced per-seat, the invoice is $99/month regardless of how many requests a customer sends. Priced on usage, the invoice is $0.002 per request, and metered billing is the part of the system that counts those requests correctly, in real time, at whatever volume the customer sends them. For the pricing-model side of this (which usage metric to pick, how to structure tiers, how usage-based pricing affects retention), see the complete guide to usage-based billing . Metered billing vs. subscription billing Subscription billing charges a fixed, recurring fee regardless of usage. The invoice is the same every month whether a customer barely touches the product or runs it constantly. Metered billing charges based on consumption, so the invoice total moves with usage. Neither is strictly better. They solve for different things. Subscription billing gives customers predictable costs and gives the vendor predictable revenue, which is why it's still the default for products with steady, bounded usage. Metered billing fits products where cost genuinely scales with consumption: infrastructure, AI inference, API platforms, where a flat fee either overcharges light users or undercharges heavy ones. Most companies don't pick one or the other outright. The common middle ground is hybrid: a flat base subscription that covers a usage allotment, with metered overage billing once a customer exceeds it. It's the structure behind most modern API and infrastructure pricing, and it's why "metered billing" and "subscription billing" are better understood as two mechanisms a pricing model can combine, not two competing categories. Do you need dedicated metering software? If you're tracking a handful of usage dimensions at low volume, you can probably get away with logging usage in your own database and running a monthly script against it. That approach breaks down once you're handling high-volume events, need aggregation in real time rather than at month-end, or have to guarantee billing accuracy at a scale where a rounding error or a dropped event turns into a real revenue or trust problem. At that point, the choice is build a metering layer in-house or adopt one as part of a billing platform. Building it yourself means owning idempotency, aggregation logic, and rating rules as a permanent piece of engineering surface area. Solvable, but it's plumbing your team maintains instead of product your team ships. Buying it means picking a platform that fits how your team actually works: some are closed, hosted-only SaaS, and that tradeoff gets more concrete once a vendor changes ownership. Take Orb, now being acquired by Adyen : teams evaluating usage-based billing platforms suddenly have to weigh a payments processor's roadmap alongside the metering feature set. Lago is open-source and self-hostable, which matters specifically for teams that want usage data to stay on their own infrastructure or need to customize pricing logic beyond what a vendor's UI exposes. For the cloud-infrastructure-specific version of this build-vs-buy question (instance metering, compute billing, multi-tenant usage tracking), see metered billing for cloud infrastructure . Metered billing in practice: real examples GitHub Copilot. In April 2026, GitHub announced it was moving Copilot off a fixed monthly allotment of "premium request units" and onto GitHub AI Credits, a token-based consumption model where usage is calculated from actual input, output, and cached token consumption at each model's listed API rate, effective June 1, 2026. The change was a direct response to agentic coding sessions consuming far more compute than a flat per-request allotment could account for: a case study in what happens when usage stops being roughly uniform and a flat-rate model starts systematically over- or under-charging. Stripe. Stripe ships metered billing as a native feature of Stripe Billing. Customers report usage via API, Stripe aggregates it against a subscription item, and the invoice reflects metered usage on top of (or instead of) a flat fee. It's a reasonable default if a team is already fully inside Stripe's payments stack and doesn't need usage data or pricing logic to live anywhere else, though attempting to replicate a genuinely complex usage-based pricing model on Stripe Billing surfaces real limitations once percentage-based fees and multi-dimensional usage enter the picture. Mistral. Mistral bills for its frontier AI models by converting API events into billable metrics with Lago, aggregating usage across dimensions like input versus output tokens and model type rather than a single flat per-token rate. It's metering with enough granularity to price each dimension of an AI product separately, not just count total tokens. Blacksmith. Blacksmith runs compute-intensive CI/CD infrastructure, a workload where cost is inherently tied to usage, not seats. Using Lago to meter and bill that usage, Blacksmith grew to 700+ paying customers and eight figures in ARR in its first year live. It's a case where the billing layer wasn't a back-office afterthought. Accurate metering was a precondition for a pricing model that could scale with a compute-heavy product at all. Key takeaways Metered billing measures usage and bills after the fact. It's a mechanism, not a pricing decision on its own. Usage-based billing is the pricing strategy; metered billing is the infrastructure that makes it possible. Subscription and metered billing aren't opposites. Most real pricing models combine a flat base with metered overage. Dedicated metering software earns its place once usage volume, real-time aggregation needs, or accuracy requirements outgrow a homegrown script. Build vs. buy is a real tradeoff, not a foregone conclusion. GitHub's 2026 move to token-based Copilot billing and Blacksmith's compute-metered CI/CD platform are both concrete evidence that metered billing isn't theoretical. It's what usage-driven products end up needing once flat pricing stops matching actual cost. Lago meters usage as event data in real time , up to 1,000,000 events per second, and is open-source and self-hostable for teams that want that infrastructure on their own terms.

title: How to get the best out of Q4: Tips to end your year strong
summary: Prep your store for Q4 2026 with expert ecommerce tips, sales strategy, inventory planning, personalization, and new channels to boost holiday revenue.
body_text: IT'S ON 🔥 We're about to reach the most wonderful (and stressful) time of the year. The last push. The last effort. The time that can determine how good our year is going to end. And in 2026, the stakes are higher than ever: new selling channels, smarter shoppers, and more competition than we've ever seen. The long-awaited Q4 starts in a month 🤯 As you know, most customers put all their energy and time into buying products and services during the last part of the year, so businesses should use these buying habits to their advantage. In this post, we'll cover: - How to organize your business before the rush hits - Sales and marketing strategies to maximize the Q4 window - New selling channels to reach more customers in 2026 Here are some tips that will help you get ready and cross the finish line by the end of the year. Don't underestimate the importance of being organized If you want your Q4 season to run smoothly, it's essential to be exceptionally organized 📅 The best thing you can do is look back to understand where you stand today. Analyze how this quarter has impacted your business over the last few years, how it differs from the rest of the year, what worked before 👍 and what didn't 👎 1. Set goals What do you want to accomplish by the end of the year? 🎯 Put the numbers over the table . Set clear, ambitious, but achievable goals. The numbers back it up: U.S. online holiday sales reached $257.8 billion in 2025, a 6.8% increase over 2024. And the 2025 holiday season was the first ever to cross $1 trillion in total retail sales. Use these benchmarks as a reference when setting your targets, and don't leave Q4 without a clear number to aim for. 2. Prepare a budget Make sure you set up a plan and stick to the budget 💰 Operating costs may increase during this peak season due to higher shipping costs and other factors. It's important to stay on budget while making sure you're getting maximum profit. 3. Watch your stock Stocking up adequately for the fourth quarter is more important than you might think. Inventory is an aspect that's often overlooked, sometimes salespeople don't factor in actual sales projections when deciding what needs restocking. Considering delivery times, shipping costs, and planning in advance is critical. While it's important to stock up and meet expected high demand, you also need to be careful not to overstock. 4. Put your customer first Companies that focus too much on numbers and statistics sometimes forget about the customer. That's why it's important to look at how your customers actually interact with your store. - Offer flexible payment options. The more ways a customer has to pay you, the better. - Look at what customers said last year and what they're saying about your business now 🗣️ Evaluate the positive and negative reviews equally. - Analyze how you can improve the customer experience during this busy time, and plan how you'll implement those improvements. ‍ Prepare your sales and marketing strategies For marketing and sales teams, this is the most important time of the year 📈 Anticipating and paving the way for them will have a positive impact on your business. Let's look at some options: 1. Plan your marketing calendar The fourth quarter is fast-moving, especially in e-commerce. Within a small window of time, sellers have the opportunity to get their products to customers on Halloween , Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Christmas , and more. By making a plan for each of these occasions, you can make the most of every opportunity to increase sales. Use the holiday calendar as a planning tool, and match these dates with the strong offers you tested earlier in the year 😉 In 2026, also map out your channel strategy, which dates are best for TikTok Shop live events, which products go on Amazon for Prime fall deals, and which campaigns live on your own store. 2. Encourage customers to visit frequently Since consumers are in a buying mood during the last few months of the year, encourage them to come back often! Give them reasons to check out your shop, pull out their wallet, and buy your products. Use discount codes or coupons that expire within a set number of hours or days. You can also give them a coupon redeemable at a later date that pulls them back for a second purchase. 3. New and trendy products Q4 is a good time to test new, innovative, or interesting products. Your competitors will do the same, or introduce higher-quality products in the same category to compete. Pricing and promotional strategy also play a big role during the holidays. Focus your efforts on items with the highest potential to stand out, whether they solve a specific problem or are simply visually appealing. 4. Host events that attract customers To boost sales, organize events that bring in both loyal and new customers. This gives customers a chance to see your exclusive seasonal items, and gives your team a chance to connect with loyal fans and make a strong first impression on new ones. A happy customer is more likely to spend more on your business, and will promote your brand to their friends and family. 5. Fries with your burger? Bundling complementary or similar products into a single package and marking them "Frequently Bought Together" is a popular resource for selling online 🍔🍟. Bundling drives impulse buys as customers feel they're getting a great deal, which increases average order value and revenue. To succeed with bundling this Q4, get comfortable packaging complementary products together and displaying them clearly in your store, so customers don't have to scroll through multiple listings to find each item. 6. Test your offers in advance Go into the season with strong offers that attract new customers and maximize sales from existing ones. Run A/B tests on different offers and discounts to see what works best. Test multiple variations, items in a bundle, size or color options, etc. and use the results to inform your Q4 campaigns. 7. Sell where your customers already are: TikTok Shop, Amazon & beyond 📱 One of the biggest shifts heading into Q4 2026 is the rise of social commerce and new selling platforms. If you're only selling on your own store, you're leaving a massive audience on the table. The winning strategy today is omnichannel, meeting shoppers wherever they discover products. TikTok Shop has evolved into a full commerce engine in 2026. Over 65% of Gen Z shoppers now start product discovery on social video platforms rather than search engines, and TikTok Shop is where they buy. For Q4, that means running LIVE selling events during peak moments like Black Friday, partnering with creators through the affiliate program (you only pay commission on actual sales), and making sure your best gift products are optimized for TikTok's visual-first format. Products that can be shown and explained in a few seconds, personalized gifts, home goods, apparel, perform especially well. Amazon remains critical for Q4, especially for personalized and gift products. With Amazon's second Prime event landing in October and holiday traffic surging through December, sellers need to submit FBA inventory early, missing inbound deadlines can cost you the Prime badge during Cyber Week and tank visibility. Invest in short product videos (shoppers are 73% more likely to buy after watching one), and use influencer or user-generated content in your Amazon Brand Store to make listings feel more authentic and gift-ready. Consumers have shown they're willing to pay a real premium for products that feel personal and individual. The smart play in 2026 is combining all three: your own store for margins and customer ownership, Amazon for reach and Prime shoppers, and TikTok Shop for discovery and impulse buys. Each channel has its own peak moments in Q4, plan for them now rather than scrambling in November. 8. Increase sales by adding personalization Differentiation matters more than ever, and it's tough to achieve. That's why customization plays such a key role across every business, don't miss this wave 🌊 Every customer has their own needs, and the best way to meet them is customization. ‍ Customers are getting more demanding, and they're starting to demand personalized products over mass offerings. Large companies started introducing personalizable products in recent years with great success. Personalization doesn't just increase sales, it builds brand loyalty by creating something unique together with the customer. Customily has rolled out several new features in 2026 that make this easier than ever: - Multi Image Upload: lets customers add multiple photos to a single product, opening the door to richer, more personal gifts. - Multi Preview for Product Bases: shows buyers how their customization looks across different product variants before they commit, reducing hesitation and returns. - AI Filters: bring a new creative layer to personalization, letting customers apply artistic effects to their designs in seconds. - Word Search Puzzles: add a completely new product type to your catalog, personalized puzzles where shoppers enter their own names and words, turning a simple product into a meaningful custom gift. ‍ Ready to put some of these strategies to work? 🚀 This is just the tip of the iceberg, there's a lot more to explore and implement underneath. Remember: try different strategies and find out what works best for your business, since it may look different from the store next door. The clock is ticking ⏰ Don't wait any longer! Start planning your Q4 today, and give 2026 the strong finish it deserves.

title: Freedom Holding Marks New Türkiye Milestone as Freedom Yatırım Secures Brokerage License
summary: Freedom Holding Corp. is a corporation organized in the United States under the laws of the State of Nevada and is the parent company of several operating subsidiaries primarily engaged in a broad range of activities in the securities…
body_text: Freedom Holding Marks New Türkiye Milestone as Freedom Yatırım Secures Brokerage License Download as PDF August 19, 2026 ISTANBUL, Turkey, Aug. 19, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Freedom Yatırım Menkul Değerler A.Ş., a subsidiary of Freedom Holding Corp. (NASDAQ: FRHC), has received an operating license from the Capital Markets Board of Türkiye (CMB). Freedom Yatırım has become the first broadly authorized foreign brokerage firm to receive such a license in Türkiye since 1992. The license marks an important step in Freedom Holding Corp.’s expansion in Türkiye and supports its broader strategy to grow its brokerage business and international capital markets infrastructure in the country. “Receiving this operating license is an important milestone for Freedom Holding Corp. It marks our entry into the Turkish brokerage market as the first broadly authorized foreign firm to receive such a license in 34 years,” said Timur Turlov, Founder and CEO of Freedom Holding Corp. Freedom Holding Corp. operates through more than 200 offices in over 20 countries across North America, Europe, and Asia. According to its latest financial statements filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the company’s total assets stood at US$14 billion as of June 30, 2026. Brokerage remains one of its core business lines, accounting for approximately 39% of total net revenue. Freedom Yatırım will draw on Freedom Holding Corp.’s international brokerage expertise, technology, and infrastructure as it prepares to launch investment services in Türkiye. Connecting Türkiye with International Markets Freedom Yatırım plans to offer more than traditional brokerage services. Using TraderNet, Freedom Holding Corp.’s proprietary trading platform, the company intends to build infrastructure that provides two-way access between the Turkish market and international capital markets. For investors in Türkiye, the goal is to gradually broaden access to international markets through Freedom Holding Corp.’s global brokerage capabilities. Freedom Yatırım has also completed its integration with Borsa İstanbul, giving clients across the Group’s international brokerage network access to investment opportunities in the Turkish market. The network has more than 870,000 client accounts. Freedom Holding Corp. expects this infrastructure to help increase international participation in Türkiye’s capital markets and strengthen links between Borsa İstanbul and global financial markets. Building an Integrated Digital Ecosystem Freedom Holding Corp. recently completed the acquisition of a 99.32% stake in Turkish Bank A.Ş. through its subsidiary Freedom Finansal Hizmetler A.Ş. Following the acquisition, the bank’s shareholders approved the change of its trade name to Freedom Bank A.Ş. Together, Freedom Bank and Freedom Yatırım are expected to form the core of Freedom Holding Corp.’s digital financial ecosystem in Türkiye, combining banking and investment services with other digital offerings. “Our ambition in Türkiye goes beyond brokerage. We plan to build an integrated digital financial ecosystem around Freedom Bank and Freedom Yatırım, bringing banking, investment, and other digital services together over time. We will draw on our experience in Kazakhstan, where Freedom SuperApp already combines financial and everyday digital services within a single platform, while adapting the model to the needs of the Turkish market,” Turlov stated. For the local team, the next stage will be to combine the Group’s international capabilities with expertise in the Turkish market. “Türkiye is a long-term market for us. We want to combine the Group’s technology, financial strength, and international capital markets expertise with strong local knowledge to build a sustainable business here,” said Vladimir Pochekuev, Partner at Freedom Holding Corp. and Chairman of the Board of Directors of Freedom Yatırım Menkul Değerler A.Ş. Pochekuev also expressed his appreciation to the Capital Markets Board of Türkiye for its constructive and professional engagement throughout the licensing process . Preparing to Launch Operations Following receipt of its operating license, Freedom Yatırım is continuing to prepare for the launch of full-scale operations in the Turkish market. The company is conducting comprehensive system testing and finalizing its operational readiness. Freedom Yatırım intends to offer clients technology-driven, user-friendly investment services tailored to the regulatory requirements and specific needs of the Turkish market. “Türkiye has a large and increasingly sophisticated investor base, with growing interest in diversifying portfolios across markets and asset classes. Our focus will be on combining access to international markets with strong local expertise and a high standard of client service,” said Vusal Mamedov, Senior Adviser to the Board of Directors of Freedom Yatırım. About Freedom Yatırım Menkul Değerler A.Ş. Freedom Yatırım Menkul Değerler A.Ş. operates under Freedom Finansal Hizmetler A.Ş., a wholly owned subsidiary of Freedom Holding Corp. The company received approval for its establishment from the Capital Markets Board of Türkiye (CMB) in 2025 and, upon completing all regulatory requirements, obtained its operating license in 2026 to provide brokerage services in Türkiye’s capital markets. Freedom Yatırım seeks to leverage its international expertise and in-depth understanding of the Turkish market to provide investors with innovative investment solutions. About Freedom Holding Corp.
